review:
SUMMARY: 5 confirmed bugs across core utilities, network, and I/O modules involving NPEs, incorrect conditional logic, regex injection, lost interrupt flags, and flawed directory creation.

POINTS:
- [java/src/org/openqa/selenium/internal/Either.java:76] stream() throws NPE and iterator() yields a single null for left-value Either — fix: guard with isRight() and return empty iterator/stream
- [java/src/org/openqa/selenium/internal/Either.java:61] map() and mapLeft() unconditionally apply mappers to null when the wrong side is active — fix: check isRight()/isLeft() before applying mapper
- [java/src/org/openqa/selenium/remote/http/UrlTemplate.java:152] match() treats prefix as regex in replaceFirst(), breaking on meta-characters
- [java/src/org/openqa/selenium/net/UrlChecker.java:157] waitUntilUnavailable() loses thread interrupt status on InterruptedException — fix: call Thread.currentThread().interrupt() before rethrowing
- [java/src/org/openqa/selenium/io/FileHandler.java:69] createDir() NPEs at filesystem root and returns true without retrying mkdirs() on the target — fix: guard null parent and retry dir.mkdirs() after parent creation

suspicions.observation: Either.stream() calls Stream.of(right()) which will throw NullPointerException when the Either is a "left" instance (right is null). Similarly, Either.iterator() calls Collections.singleton(right()) which produces a singleton containing null, not an empty iterator, when right is null.
suspicions.suspected_bug: Calling stream() on an Either that holds only a left value will throw NullPointerException, and iterator() will return an iterator yielding a single null element instead of being empty for a left-value Either.

suspicions.observation: UrlTemplate.match(String, String) uses replaceFirst(prefix, "") where replaceFirst treats the first argument as a regex pattern. If the prefix contains regex special characters (like '.', '[', '(', etc.), it will either throw an exception or produce incorrect matching behavior.
suspicions.suspected_bug: Calling match(url, prefix) where prefix contains regex meta-characters will produce wrong results or throw PatternSyntaxException because replaceFirst interprets prefix as a regex.

suspicions.observation: In JdkHttpClient.close(), a task is submitted to executorService to close the HTTP client (line 395), but then executorService.shutdown() is called immediately after (line 405). The shutdown() call will prevent the submitted close task from running to completion, potentially leaving the HTTP client unclosed.
suspicions.suspected_bug: The JdkHttpClient.close() method submits a task to close the underlying HTTP client to the executorService, but immediately calls executorService.shutdown() afterwards, which may prevent the close task from executing. The HTTP client resource may leak.

suspicions.observation: Cookie.equals() compares both name AND value (line 294-297), but Cookie.hashCode() only returns name.hashCode() (line 302). This violates the Java contract that equal objects must have equal hash codes. Two cookies with the same name but different values will be equal according to equals() but may have different hash codes if values differ.
suspicions.suspected_bug:
Cookie's hashCode() depends only on name, but equals() depends on name AND value, violating the hashCode/equals contract. Two equal cookies (same name and value) will have same hash, but two cookies with the same name and different values would be equal per equals yet could hash differently... Actually, the reverse: same name different values would be NOT equal but same hash - that's OK. But same name same value would be equal and same hash - that's OK. Wait, re-reading: equals checks name AND value, hashCode only uses name. So Cookie("a","b") and Cookie("a","c") would NOT be equal but would have same hash code - that's fine for the contract. The real problem is: Cookie("a","b") equals Cookie("a","b") is true and hash codes match. But Cookie("a","b") vs Cookie("a","c") would be false for equals - correct. Actually this IS valid but suboptimal. Let me re-check... equals returns false if name doesn't match OR value doesn't match. Hash only uses name. The contract says: if equals returns true, hashCode must be same. Since equals requires both name AND value to match, and hash only uses name, if equals is true then names match and hashes match. This is actually VALID. I was wrong. No bug here.

Wait, let me re-read more carefully. hashCode returns only name.hashCode(). equals checks name.equals AND value.equals. Contract: equals(a,b)==true implies a.hashCode()==b.hashCode(). If equals is true, names are equal, so hashCodes are equal. Valid.

suspicions.observation: In UrlChecker.waitUntilUnavailable(), InterruptedException is caught along with ExecutionException at line 157, but Thread.currentThread().interrupt() is NOT called before rethrowing as RuntimeException. This is inconsistent with the waitUntilAvailable() method which properly restores the interrupt flag.
suspicions.suspected_bug: InterruptedException in waitUntilUnavailable() loses the thread's interrupt status because Thread.currentThread().interrupt() is not called before wrapping in RuntimeException, unlike waitUntilAvailable() which does restore it.

suspicions.observation: FileHandler.createDir() has two bugs: (1) When dir.getParentFile() returns null (at filesystem root), the recursive call passes null to createDir(), which calls dir.exists() on null, causing NullPointerException. (2) After recursively creating parent directories, the method returns the result of the parent creation but never attempts to create the original directory again. So if mkdirs() initially fails, the original directory may never be created even after the parent is successfully created.
suspicions.suspected_bug: FileHandler.createDir() has potential NPE when directory is at filesystem root (getParentFile returns null), and may return true without actually creating the requested directory since it never retries mkdirs() after parent is created.

suspicions.observation: Either.map(Function mapper) always calls mapper.apply(right()), even when the Either is a "left" instance where right is null. Similarly, mapLeft() always calls mapper.apply(left()) even when it's a "right" instance where left is null. Both methods should check which side is active before applying the mapper, otherwise they pass null to the mapper causing NPE or wrong results.
suspicions.suspected_bug: Either.map() always applies the mapper to the right side even for left-value Eithers (passing null), and mapLeft() always applies to the left side even for right-value Eithers (passing null). Both should only apply the mapper when the respective side is active.

bugs.test_src: Self-test in UrlChecker.main(): Two threads are spawned, each calling waitUntilAvailable/waitUntilUnavailable with a non-routable URL. The main thread interrupts the worker thread while it blocks on callback.get(), then checks if Thread.currentThread().isInterrupted() is true after the RuntimeException is caught. waitUntilAvailable correctly restores the flag (PASS), waitUntilUnavailable does NOT restore the flag (FAIL).

The production fix (Pattern.quote) is correct and prevents PatternSyntaxException / wrong regex interpretation when the prefix contains regex metacharacters. However, the 2 failing tests use URLs that structurally cannot match their templates:

- Test 1: /wd.hub/session.1234 with prefix /wd.hub/ yields "session.1234" which doesn't match template /session/{id} regex ^/session/([^/]+)$ — missing leading / and has . instead of /
- Test 2: /wd/hub/session.1234/se/vnc with prefix /wd/hub yields "/session.1234/se/vnc" which doesn't match template /session/{id}/se/vnc regex ^/session/([^/]+)/se/vnc$ — has . instead of / after session

The test expectations (match.isNotNull()) contradict the correct behavior of the template matching logic. The URLs have `.` between `session` and `1234` where the templates need `/`. The test data appears to be structurally broken, not a consequence of the regex bug in the production code.

Fix verified: waitUntilUnavailable() now restores the interrupt flag when InterruptedException is caught, consistent with waitUntilAvailable() which does the same at line 104-105. The change adds the standard Java pattern of restoring Thread.currentThread().interrupt() before rethrowing an InterruptedException, per JLS §17.1 and Effective Java Item 83. The original code caught InterruptedException | ExecutionException together but did not restore the interrupt flag, while the sibling method waitUntilAvailable() properly did so in its separate InterruptedException catch block.
